latest_nl_proof:
Fix a real number r with r \le 1/4, and let n be any positive integer.

Since r \le 1/4, we have
4r \le 1.

Now n \ge 1. We compare n^{4r} with n.

If n=1, then n^{4r}=1=n, so certainly n^{4r} \le n.

If n>1, then \ln n>0. From 4r \le 1 we get
(4r)\ln n \le \ln n.
Exponentiating both sides yields
n^{4r}=e^{(4r)\ln n} \le e^{\ln n}=n.

Thus in all cases,
n^{4r} \le n.

Also,
2n+1-n = n+1 > 0,
so n \le 2n+1.

Combining these inequalities gives
n^{4r} \le n \le 2n+1.
Hence
2n+1 \ge n^{4r}.

Since n was arbitrary, this holds for every positive integer n.
role_in_parent: Elementary inequality needed to verify the quadratic witness for all exponents r <= 1/4.
statement_nl: Let r be a real number with r \le \tfrac14. Then for every positive integer n, one has 2n+1 \ge n^{4r}.

domain_restrictions: r is a real number and satisfies r ≤ 1/4
Exponentiation n^{4r} is interpreted as real exponentiation of a positive base (base n > 0 guarantees well-definedness)
quantifier_order: For all r ∈ ℝ with r ≤ 1/4

variables.name: r
variables.role: parameter, universally quantified over reals satisfying domain restriction

variables.name: n
variables.role: universal variable ranging over positive integers
